Her laughter cut cleanly through the vastness of the hangar. The technician frowned and turned back to his console. Mu’s eyes, however, lingered on a faint scratch near the muzzle—eerily similar to the acid scar that had marred her old Hellfire Cannon after tangling with Zerg bio-acid.

Before she could pull her hand away, that familiar mark dragged the past right back in front of her—memories flooding in like a tide.

It was in the Zeta System asteroid belt. She was still in the Falcon Squad’s red-and-black armor, the Hellfire’s cooling tube freshly punctured by a Ravager’s sting. The Hive’s bioplasmic shell throbbed in the distance, dark green Zerg blood raining against her visor like stormwater. Yet she was yelling into the comms: “Aim for the folds in that rotten meat! Give me three seconds to reload!”

By the time the third shell fired, her shoulder—already torn by Zerg claws—dislocated violently from the recoil, throwing her into a floating debris field. But through the smoke and chaos, she saw the Hive’s shell rip open like rotten fabric, countless smaller creatures spilling out only to be vaporized in the blast wave. Pushing herself up, her back plating soaked in blood, she grinned at the still-smoking cannon: “See that? Now that’s how you open a can.”

“Mu?” The technician’s voice hauled her back into the present. “Energy calibration is complete. Care to test it?”

She pulled her hand away, the cold of the OR-DX lingering on her skin. Mu flexed her right arm—the old injury still ached when it rained, a permanent reminder of her dance with the Zerg. “Let’s do it.” She hefted the cannon eagerly; the barrel was heavier than her old Hellfire, yet it felt familiar in a way that took her back to the first time she’d held a rifle.

The first shot roared out, shaking the hangar lights. Mu staggered half a step, muscles in her arm coiling tight—but instead of backing away as the tech expected, she leaned into the recoil, angling the barrel upward, her eyes shining brighter than the muzzle’s blue flare. “Not bad. Easier than cracking a Hive.”

The technician was already jotting down data without looking up. “Missions in the Fourth Fleet are ten times deadlier than Zerg clean-up duty.”

“Perfect,” Mu replied, returning the cannon to its mount. Her fingert brushed once more over that scratch—like an old scar. “I was getting bored.”

Footsteps echoed from the corridor: Ulysses from the Fourth Fleet was already waiting outside to escort her to the barracks. As Mu followed, she passed a viewing port and saw the starships docked outside—their black hulls shimmering in stardust like a pack of lurking beasts. She remembered the badge Commander Ariya had given her when she left the Falcons, engraved with a single word: Storm. That badge was still in her kit bag. The left side of her new Fourth Fleet uniform, though, remained bare.

“Heard our next operation is pushing into uncharted space?” Mu called ahead to Ulysses.

“If you’re scared, just say so. I won’t judge,” Ulysses tossed back without turning, a playful tone in her voice.

Mu smiled, a fierce light igniting in her expression. “Scared? I was just thinking of giving the OR-DX a nickname. Like I called the Hellfire ‘Old Trusty.’”

The lights grew brighter at the end of the corridor, stretching her shadow long and sharp, like a blade unsheathed. The memory of fighting Zerg still burned in her bones, but now—more than anything—she looked forward to what lay ahead. The Fourth Fleet’ airlock slid open before her, revealing not the darkness of space, but a deeper, hotter darkness: one waiting beyond the known. Her palm tingled, already craving the tremor of the trigger.
story.STORY_FLEET_614:
It did not appear in human form. As the Shadow Will breached the third defensive line and corrosive acid ate away at the starship’s energy shields, It materialized abruptly before the bridge’s main viewscreen.

“What... is that?” a lieutenant stammered. On the screen, the vanguard swarm of Shadow Will was being torn apart by an invisible force. Shadowy forms melted like snow meeting flame upon contact with the white radiance—vanishing without even a wisp of smoke.

Its movements were precise and efficient; every strike severed a core node of the Shadow Will. The shadow energy, which even the Empire’s most advanced plasma cannons could not harm, seemed as fragile as paper before It. When the last of the Shadow Will dissolved into light, the command deck fell into a brief silence. Someone whispered, “Like... a ferryman of souls.”

The name “Karon” began to spread.

No one knew where It came from, or why It appeared on the front lines against the Shadow Will. No one had ever heard It speak. They only remembered how, after each battle, that indistinct yet brilliant glow would turn toward the command platform—as if confirming the victory. Technicians who tried to scan Its structure captured only chaotic, high-dimensional energy readings. The analysis report concluded: “Non-carbon-based lifeform. Neither machine nor flesh. Most likely a projection of Will of Divinity.”

The first invitation for Karon to join came during an ambush at a derelict relay station. The flagship’s engines were frozen; the ship itself was on the verge of falling into a rift abyss. Then It appeared—slashing through reality with a luminous scythe, enveloping the entire station within a barrier of sacred runes. A man-made miracle, unlike anything ever witnessed. All shadows and corruption crumbled inch by inch under the blinding flood of purifying light.

“We need you!” Eric yelled over the alarm blares and shockwaves. “The Imperial Elite Fleet is tasked with destroying the Shadow Will. No one is better suited than you—”

The light hesitated for half a second. Just as Eric thought there would be no reply, Karon pointed toward a set of coordinates on the star chart—the suspected location of the Alpha System Hive.

And so, It joined the Fourth Fleet.

Gnarculi assigned It the innermost docking bay, modifying the energy interfaces to harmonize with Its holy spectrum. Crew members walking by would instinctively slow their steps, watching the glow hover silently within the berth. At times, golden sparks drifted from Its form and fell to the floor, causing tiny luminous vines to sprout from the metal deck. Some speculated It was a guardian from an ancient civilization; others called It a messenger of the gods. A few rookies even left offerings at the entrance—until the captain put a stop to it.

Karon remained silent and detached. Only when battle alarms blared and Shadow Will neared did the light sharpen, the scythe’s gleam piercing the chamber’s darkness.

During one patrol, they encountered a beast large enough to swallow a destroyer. Conventional weapons were useless. But it was no match for Karon’s sudden eruption of blade formations—countless interweaving arcs of light that carved holy seals like spiderwebs across the massive shadow-corrupted body. As the creature collapsed and disintegrated, one soldier glimpsed what seemed like a skeletal, humanoid form within the mist. But when he looked again, there was only pure light, leaping and flowing beyond mortal understanding.

After that battle, energy monitors recorded abnormal fluctuations for the first time.

“Do you get tired, too?” Aiolia murmured to himself, gazing out the viewport. He expected no answer.

Yet that very night, the glowing vines spreading from Karon’s berth bloomed with silver flowers, and firefly-like lights drifted past the crew’s windows—as though gently comforting every lonely soul nearby.

The Fourth Fleet’s combat logs regarding Karon were always brief:
“Coordinate X73: Shadow Will cluster cleared.”
“Coordinate M19: High-value target eliminated.”

No additional commentary. Much like Its very existence—a light against the darkness, pure and steadfast, veiled in profound mystery.
story.STORY_FLEET_615:
On the colossal holographic admission board of the Galactic Empire Conservatory, Aiolia's name blazed atop the rankings in radiant gold, stamped with the indelible mark of "Highest Overall Score." Across Warfare Star, voices rose in celebration of this prodigy's achievement—yet none knew the fiery crucible of brotherhood that had forged this brilliance, nor the shadow-streaked youth who stood eternally at his side.

Sector Seven's anti-gravity training grounds bore witness to their odyssey. Each dawn, as the first interstellar light speared the dome's crystalline canopy, Aiolia would already be hunched over the tactical simulator, his pianist's fingers dancing across holographic controls. Quantum entanglement matrices unfolded beneath his touch, virtual battalions moving with clockwork precision—flawless maneuvers that drew admiring murmurs from observing instructors.

Teda arrived as the countdown beeps faded, his footfalls quaking the alloy floor. Without ceremony, he'd crank the gravity generator to its limit, heft training rigs triple his mass, and begin. Sweat carved canyons down his granite jaw, pooling on steel plates that trembled with each rep. Where Aiolia wove elegance, Teda authored earthquakes.

The day of their final trial, Aiolia cleaned his particle pistol with monastic focus. "No holding back today," he said, lenses flashing. Teda responded by tearing his sleeve free, exposing the relic of their childhood—a jagged scar from ruins where he'd shielded Aiolia from collapsing plasteel. The alarm blared.

Aiolia became quicksilver, slipping through laser grids like a specter, each shot a synapse-fire reflex. Teda raged through the course like a siege engine, shattering alloy barriers with bare fists until the air itself groaned. Then—catastrophe. Aiolia's tactical goggles died mid-leap, plunging him into void. Teda's body intercepted the searing laser meant for his friend's spine, flesh sizzling.

Afterward, as med-nanites stitched his arm, Teda tossed Aiolia a backup chip. "Perfect tactics need fallbacks," he grunted. "Next time, I'm your eyes."

Years burned away in this alchemy of rivalry and devotion. Aiolia crouched beside exhausted Teda, debugging his tactical reports with surgical precision. Teda hauled Aiolia through marathon training collapses, an unyielding crutch. They'd brawl over flanking maneuvers, then embrace laughing after conquering impossible drills.

The Elite Fleet trials came. Aiolia dominated theory with fractal-strategy genius while Teda rewrote physical records—his sprint shaking decade-old leaderboards. The final gauntlet: Death Canyon's antimatter labyrinth. Aiolia's reactivated goggles mapped trap cycles, his voice calm in Teda's ear: "Left vector unstable—pivot!" Teda became a living bulwark, tanking energy surges, demolishing laser grids to carve a path. At the finish, he slowed. Let Aiolia cross first. His smile held no envy, only pride.

Under the victory bonfire's ember rain, they melted their training badges into twin pendants. As the fleet's engines roared to life beyond the flames, the unspoken truth shimmered between them—this was but the first stanza of their symphony. The Shadow Will's storm gathered at the galaxy's rim, and where one star blazed, the other would always burn brighter in answer.

"True strength is never solitary—it's the light two torches cast when held side by side."
story.STORY_FLEET_616:
To the Commander of the 4th Fleet, 

Conventional magnetic confinement fields in the void turbulence zone are like trying to catch a storm with a fishing net. At 1.8 Tesla, the magnetic field lines shatter upon colliding with dark matter particles, causing the engine’s nuclear fusion confinement time to plummet from the standard 4.2 seconds to a mere 0.7 seconds. Every teleport risks self-destruction. 

But the simulation experiments led by Ulysses at the observation station told a different story. She didn’t rely on complex energy matrices. Instead, she cut the cooling pipes of a decommissioned teleport engine into three segments, filled them with stardust-sourced monocrystalline silicon fragments, and arranged them into a Fresnel lens array. Monitoring data showed the energy frequency—which previously jumped 17 times per second—stabilized at 2.3 Hz, with leakage suppressed below 0.003%. It was like placing an invisible buffer on a raging energy flow, allowing the deuterium-core fusion to “breathe steadily” within the turbulence. 

Her toolbox is always full of curiosities: small spheres ground from discarded neodymium magnets that can detect quantum tunneling effects three seconds in advance; a bracelet she wound with 376 turns of hair-thin superconducting coil because it “hears the heartbeat of energy vorticity.” On the energy model diagram Narin drafted for her, those jagged waveforms the tech division dismissed as noise were actually intentional safety redundancies. When energy density in the turbulence zone exceeds 8.9×10¹² joules per cubic meter, these waveforms trigger a drainage protocol—like airbags inflating. 

Don’t be fooled by her glittering crystals. Last week, while repairing the energy analyzer at the Meri station, she replaced the superconducting joints with nickel-iron alloy hammered from meteorites. By adjusting the lattice spacing to 0.38 nanometers, she increased the instrument’s sensitivity by 47%. The way this girl handles energy is less like brute-force engineering and more like taming a wild horse—guiding it gently to her rhythm. 

Respectfully, 
Empire 7th Fleet, Meri 

As the projection of the letter faded, Ulysses was crouched inside the 4th Fleet’s engine conduit, hanging strings of shimmering crystal shards along the energy lines. Each one clinked like a wind chime, a delicate sound stark against the roar of machinery. 

“Ms. Ulysses,” the Chief Engineer adjusted his glasses, his tone weary. “You can’t just modify the fleet’s energy conduits—” 

“Yes, I can!” She sprang up, holding a palm-sized regulator with a pitted shell and a small glow-in-the-dark sticker—courtesy of Narin, who said it made things easier to find in the dark. “Watch this,” she clipped it onto the main console. The energy readings, which had been flailing like a frantic heartbeat, suddenly steadied. “Narin calculated that three turns of these gears are just enough to lock down the ‘irritable points’ of the turbulence.” 

Before she could finish, a sharp alarm cut through the engine room. On the console, the energy curve of the turbulence zone spiked into the red. Gamma photon counts from fusion broke 1.2×10⁹ per second. The Chief Engineer reached for the emergency button—but Ulysses stopped him. 

“Wait.” She tuned the regulator to a 2.4 GHz resonance, her fingers flying across the panel. “Angle the eddy current in the superconducting coil 11.3 degrees against the energy vorticity. It’s like putting a speed bump in front of a rampaging flow.” 

Something miraculous happened: the wild energy curve was pressed down by an invisible hand, falling steadily at 0.02% per second. The temperature in the engine room dropped by 1.7 degrees Celsius. The main console settled at 897.6 gigajoules. The crystals along the conduit hummed softly, and the refracted light spots on the screen formed a lopsided smiling face. 

“See?” Ulysses plucked a crystal and held it to the light. “They’re praising me.” The Chief Engineer stared, speechless. The light in her eyes seemed brighter than the energy glow on the displays. 

Her communic buzzed—a message from Narin. Ulysses looked down to reply, a smudge of fluorescent marker still at the corner of her mouth: 

“You overshot the dark energy coupling coefficient by 0.002. You owe me a supernova ice cream—the kind made from engine waste heat.”
story.STORY_FLEET_617:
BD-5l, a world buried deep in the Phalanx District, where even starlight dares not reach. An eternal night, thick as a burial shroud, smothers the entire surface, while stardust condenses into a motionless, thin mist in the oppressive dark. Dark red magma seeps silently from tectonic scars, flowing in sluggish rivers. The only structure to break the desolation is a prison carved from the wreckage of the Radiance. Three centuries ago, this cruiser of the Seventh Fleet was a silver-white bastion of the galactic defense line. Now, only half its rust-eaten hull remains, driven into the ashen soil. The ship's bow emblem is scorched black by magma, its armor plates webbed with cracks from endless tectonic groans. Only the bridge's observation window stubbornly holds the holy radiance of Karon from a bygone era, now serving as the prison's main gate. On rare occasions, a passerby might see dust coalescing into a pale golden haze within that enduring light.

Few remember that this was once the primary battlefield of the Shadow Defense Line War.

It was here, before his service with the Fourth Fleet, that Karon fought for nine days and nights without respite. Warships of the Seventh Fleet were torn asunder by tectonic fury, some swallowed by lava, others dashed against rock layers. With a light blade in hand, Karon charged into the deepest tectonic veins. Star-iron crystals shattered under his feet as shadow power coiled up the blade and onto his chest. He poured every ounce of his holy energy into the planet's veins, weaving a golden seal to imprison Liser within the planetary core—but not before the shadow left a faint, perpetual purple scar over his heart.

In the aftermath, the Empire discovered Liser could not be truly destroyed. Attempts to bombard the core with holy main-cannons caused the planet to convulse—magma fountained kilometers high, scorching fleet shields. Even when its outer form was severed, the shadow's fragments would seep back through tectonic fissures, slowly reassembling. In the end, the Empire had no choice but to designate the world a "Prison Ground," sealing Liser deep below forever.

That was, until Professor Dexter's survey ship breached the silence. Standing at the magma's edge in his protective suit, his instruments suddenly screamed—a psychic echo from the tectonic veins had climbed the probe to his screen, twisting into dark, shifting patterns. "This is no ordinary shadow energy," Dexter murmured, his glasses reflecting the frantic data curves, his tone barely containing his fervor. "It can ravage the mind... more effectively than any torture device."

The Galactic Empire swiftly approved his expansion proposal. No one believed the Empire acted out of mercy—their goal was never "detention," but "elimination." They would use Liser's psychic echoes to break the will of every prisoner sent here.

The first to arrive were interstellar pirates who had massacred three colonial worlds. The night before their incarceration, they roared in their cages, pounding star-iron bars with bloody fists. By the next day, they were broken. Some clung to the bars, weeping, swearing they saw the ghosts of children they had burned standing in the dark. Others curled in corners, beating their heads against the walls, screaming, "Make it stop chanting." Karon watched silently through the energy barriers. In the gloom, he could almost see invisible particles rising from tectonic fissures, gently winding around the prisoners' heads—Liser's psychic echoes, forever lingering in the eternal night.

Professor Dexter repurposed the holy sealing array into a psychic conduction network. Substances drawn from the tectonic veins now crawled through conduits into every cell. No torture devices, no electric grids—as long as Liser's echoes remained, even the most brutal villains would eventually break. Once, a night patrol soldier saw Dexter calibrating his instruments, the brainwave curves on the screen twisting into tangled knots. From the darkness came a faint, whispering hum—Liser's voice, hidden within the psychic echoes, spreading through the conduits.

At such times, the scar over Karon's heart throbbed with heat. He knew then that Liser had never submitted. Its psychic echoes were never mere leakage, but a quiet absorption of the prisoners' fear. That despair and hatred was feeding the shadow in the abyss. Below the unending night, magma still surged in the fissures, and at the edges of the seal's golden light, a faint trace of black had begun to spread.

This planet was never just a prison. Karon gazed into the endless dark, his fingers tightening around the hilt of his light blade. He had trapped Liser's body, but failed to seal its will. Those echoes, hidden deep in the darkness, were quietly spreading along the tectonic veins, turning the entire world into Liser's hunting ground. Beyond the eternal night, the galaxy still shone bright, but here, wrapped in its black shroud, the whispers of the nemesis shadow only grew stronger in the silence.
story.STORY_FLEET_618:
Legend tells of an ancient priest of Earth—Ireland, in the age of myth—named Thorne. He was meant to wield the ceremonial "Soul-Rending Claw," a blade forged from the bone of a great bear sacrificed on Samhain night, its tips twined with thorns from the primordial wilds. Intended as a Soul-Calming Artifact, it could slice through the chaos between life and death, guiding lost spirits to rest. 

But Thorne coveted the vitality lingering in the consciousness of the dead. He sought to use the Claw’s thorned edge to tear open the barriers of the departed’s minds and seize that essence—to rule over both life and death. 

On one Samhain night, he secretly anointed the Claw with dust from human bones and chanted the soul-calming rites in reverse. As he did, the Claw grew searingly hot. Thorns burst from its tip, coiling around his wrist like living things. Ceremonial flames surged, swallowing the Claw and lashing into his mind—tearing his consciousness in two. One half fused with the burning thorn-claw; the other was cast into the Samhain Rift beneath the ritual fire: a dark tear at the edge of life and death, haunted by the worn fragments of long-faded souls. 

Uncounted years passed. The Claw, carrying Thorne’s consciousness, traveled with Irish migrants to the Americas. Millennia later, as mankind reached for the stars, it was cataloged as an "Ancient Earth Relic" and shipped to a colony world. There it lay—until a gravitational wave from a passing black hole stirred it. The bone blade glowed with eerie green light, its thorns dissolving into a stream of radiance. From it, Thorne’s consciousness finally reformed, a ghost adrift in the cosmos. 

Now he wanders the "Forgotten Place"—a graveyard of derelict starships—hunting those with fragile minds. His Claw glows with soul-green light, weaving cruel illusions: a loved one left on Earth, a pet from a colony childhood. When his targets draw near, he slashes through their mental defenses, the thorns at the Claw’s tip hooking and gathering their scattered consciousness into glowing orbs—his nourishment. 

Even consciousness-criminals imprisoned by the Empire are not safe. Some hide amid the wreckage, only to be dragged out as thorned claws pierce through metal and tear their souls away. 

Veteran starfarers claim Thorne awaits the "Interstellar Samhain," when the Samhain Rift will widen. On that day, he will use the power of a black hole to sharpen the Soul-Rending Claw enough to slice through the consciousness-boundary of the entire universe—and devour the minds of every star. 

Now, children on colony worlds dare not speak his name. Parents place star-candy on windowsills as "false offerings." The elders say Thorne cares nothing for sweetness—but the scent of sugar may trick him into thinking no fresh minds remain in that home.
story.STORY_FLEET_619:
In the holographic briefing chamber of the Imperial military outpost, Ouros watched as pale blue tactical schematics unfolded before him. “Tagnias, grid X-73,” the Admiral’s voice was a low rumble through the projection. His finger traced the star chart toward a planet veiled in violet nebular dust. “Seventeen recovery teams lost in three months. All were searching for the core component of the Transcendence Project—Supercore Luminite.” 

Ouros’s hand drifted instinctively to the combat knife at his hip, a gesture habitual to his concentration. He had heard whispers about Tagnias, though the official records listed it only as a “resource-rich world,” with no mention of disappearances. “Any anomalies in their final transmissions?” he asked. 

The Admiral triggered a distorted audio clip. Beneath the static, a faint wind could be heard—and something else, a low hum like the chime of resonating crystal. “This interference was present in every signal, right before they went silent.” The holographic figure paused meaningfully. “There’s more. Our analysts compared planetary data. Tagnias’s magnetic field, atmospheric composition, even the fluctuation patterns of its surface... all closely mirror Solaris.” 

Ouros’s eyes narrowed on the violet haze encircling Tagnias on the map. Solaris—the legends were clear. A world that could disrupt machinery, some said even sense human consciousness. No expedition had ever fully charted it. “My mission is to investigate the disappearances, not to extract Supercore Luminite. Correct?” His voice was level, deliberate. 

“Confirmed,” the Admiral nodded. “Maintain open comms. Detect anything unusual, you pull out immediately. Remember—find the cause, determine if the planet is a threat to the Imperial Fleet. Do not let the value of Supercore Luminite cloud your judgment. And do not venture beyond the three-kilometer mark into the canyon.” 

Six hours later, Ouros’s dropship broke orbit over Tagnias. During atmospheric entry, the first anomaly registered: the violet stellar mist outside his viewport didn’t scatter randomly—it flowed around the hull in deliberate, coherent patterns. His instrument panels, though reading nominal, showed a subtle tremor—a consistent 0.2 Hz oscillation beyond baseline. It was the exact same mechanical interference pattern documented in every Solaris report. 

When the landing pod settled at the edge of the Pulsing Canyon, Ouros didn’t immediately exit. Through external cameras, he observed the terrain: silvery-blue soil glowing faintly, yielding softly underfoot. Where his probes left prints, amber-yellow specks of light slowly seeped upward, like stars blooming from the ground. More unsettling were the formations of Supercore Luminite embedded in the canyon walls—semi-transparent crystals veined with pulsating amber light, their rhythm slowly, imperceptibly, syncing with his own heartbeat. 

This is no coincidence, he thought, activating his suit’s full sensor suite. Scans detected unknown particles drifting in the atmosphere, their spectral signature a near-perfect match for the silicon-based “memory particles” recorded on Solaris—entities capable of retaining environmental imprints. He stepped out, boots sinking into the luminous ground. As his gloved fingers brushed the canyon wall, a faint warmth radiated through the material—a thermal transfer pattern identical to Solaris’s purported ability to sense living presence. 

Moving deeper along the canyon, Ouros found three precisely carved grooves in the rock face—uniformly spaced, their depth matching the exact incision profile of Imperial resource harvesters. It was as if the planet itself was mimicking human technology. Remembering the final footage from the lost teams, he froze, capturing an image of the grooves. At that moment, the silvery-blue glow along the grooves’ edges brightened—pulsing in perfect sync with his respirator. 

Without warning, his comms crackled to life. A fragmented image flickered on his display—one of the missing collectors, his own hand outstretched toward the same grooves. The sensor lights on the man’s suit shifted from green to the same silvery-blue now reflected on Ouros’s own HUD. His pulse quickened. In one fluid motion, he retreated, fingers hovering over the pod’s recall switch. 

He didn’t panic, but his eyes swept the area. At the far end of the canyon, three long marks converged into a starburst pattern etched into the ground. At its center, a cluster of Supercore Luminite shone with unusual intensity—and the last known coordinates of every missing team pointed directly toward it. They didn’t just get lost, Ouros realized. They were guided. Lured toward the heart of this place. 

As he triggered the pod’s recall sequence, he noticed the amber specks in the soil suddenly align into a sharp, straight path—a luminous trail leading from his feet directly to the ship’s hatch, as though the very ground was directing his exit. Before the hatch sealed, he cast one last look toward the canyon: the grooves in the rock were slowly sealing shut, the Luminite’s glow dimming. Only the central point of the starburst pattern continued to pulse, a single unwavering eye in the gathering dark. 

Back in the Imperial Command Center, Ouros filed a comprehensive report. He cataloged 21 environmental and energetic parameters shared by Tagnias and Solaris, attached visual records of the grooves and particle readings, and included a critical note: “The planet communicates—through light patterns in the Luminite and particulate arrangements in the soil. The missing weren’t eliminated. They were receiving data. It remains unknown what effect this transmission has on human consciousness. Recommend immediate suspension of all mining operations. Tagnias displays a degree of sentient activity exceeding even Solaris.” 

While the Admiral reviewed the findings, Ouros stood silently, his gaze fixed once more on the stellar map. Beneath his boots, traces of silvery-blue soil still clung, the amber lights within them flickering faintly—a ghostly echo from the planet, and an unspoken promise that this mystery was far from over.
story.STORY_FLEET_621:
Legend has it that on the edge of the galactic spiral arm, the planet Aier was once a jewel wrapped in blue-green energy crystals. The civilization of this planet was built upon the star core crystals—not only the core energy source powering floating cities and interstellar voyages, but also the very origin of life that maintained atmospheric stability and nourished the planet’s ecosystem. For three thousand years, the people of Aier guarded the star core crystal veins, extracting energy with gentle technology and living in symbiosis with their world, until the sudden “Crystal Depletion Catastrophe” struck.

The disaster began at dawn three hundred standard years ago. At that time, Aier’s main vein suddenly erupted in energy chaos, and the star core crystals lost their activity in a short period, turning into dull rubble. Without energy supply, floating cities plummeted, protective shields failed, exposing the surface to cosmic radiation, farmlands withered, rivers froze, and even the oxygen circulation system vital for life was on the verge of collapse. Aier’s scientists exhausted all reserve energy trying to activate backup veins, only to discover that the depletion was a chain reaction triggered by interstellar energy waves—something Aier’s technology alone could not reverse. Despair spread like a cold current, and the high council even began drafting an interstellar migration plan, but it stalled due to insufficient spaceship energy.

Just as Aier was about to be swallowed by darkness, a silver-white fleet appeared in the starry sky—the Galactic Empire’s interstellar expedition team. They had originally come to observe cosmic wonders, but when passing by Aier, detected the energy anomaly and SOS signal. The expedition’s captain, an experienced interstellar diplomat, saw through holographic projection the emaciated Aierians huddling for warmth in makeshift shelters, and immediately decided to defy the Empire’s default principle of “non-interference in alien affairs” to extend a helping hand to Aier.

“Energy is a shared gift of the universe; it should not have exclusive boundaries.” This statement by the captain was later engraved on Aier’s gratitude monument. The expedition brought with them the Empire’s advanced conversion technology—a device capable of transforming dark matter from the universe into stable energy. They not only left behind three core converters, but also dispatched an engineering team to personally teach the Aierians how to calibrate the equipment and build an energy transmission network. To adapt the technology to Aier’s ecosystem, the captain even led the team deep into abandoned veins to search for residual energy in the star core crystals, eventually developing a crystal regeneration catalyst that revived some of the veins.

Three months later, when the first converted energy illuminated Aier’s main city, blue-green light once again bathed the planet. The people of Aier embraced each other in tears, holding fragments of the revitalized star core crystals and bowing deeply to the expedition team. The captain, however, simply waved her hand and presented the Aier council with an energy chip engraved with the Empire’s emblem: “Remember this mutual aid, not a debt. When you have the ability, pass on this sharing to civilizations in need.”

On the day the expedition departed, the people of Aier turned out in full to see them off, hanging necklaces made from star core crystals around each team member’s neck. Each necklace stored Aier’s coordinates and their sincerest blessings. To commemorate this cross-galactic aid, the Aier council designated the expedition’s departure date as “Star Grace Day.” Every year on this day, Aier selects its finest envoys to travel on ships equipped with improved star energy conversion technology to planets across the galaxy—not only presenting the Empire with the most precious star core crystals as thanks, but also actively providing energy technology support to resource-poor worlds, spreading the captain’s philosophy of “shared energy, united galaxy” to every corner of the universe.

Three hundred years have passed, and “Star Grace Day” has become a galaxy-wide celebration of inter-civilizational gratitude. Aier’s envoys, bearing energy badges symbolizing sharing, have set foot on thousands of planets. Their ships are always stocked with emergency energy and technical blueprints, ready to help civilizations in crisis at any time. The energy chip left by the captain is still preserved in Aier’s sanctuary to this day—not only a legacy of technology, but a promise across time and space, reminding all civilizations: the survival of the universe depends on selfless assistance and sincere gratitude.
story.STORY_FLEET_620:
“Lose to the Zerg, and only two fates await you—you end your life in acid and fangs, or you live out your days paralyzed, never to hold a rifle or stand again.” These were the last words Welly heard from a comrade before his capture in the Zeta System campaign. As the Zerg acid ate into his left arm, and his consciousness flickered, he saw a Zerg engineer dragging him toward a slime-covered bio-pod. A third, grimmer outcome flashed through his mind: being carved into experimental scrap. 

When his eyes opened again, he was lying on a cold metal slab. His left arm was now a mechanical limb pulsing with violet light, and his spine was interlaced with fine bio-wires that squirmed beneath his skin like a nest of worms. “Subject 73, Grusen resurrection protocol successfully adapted.” 

Welly fought against the control, but his body was no longer his own. The wires were tied to the Zerg's neural network, and whenever he resisted, a searing pain would shoot through his mechanical arm, forcing it to snap up an energy rifle and train its sights on fellow humans—on the very soldiers he had once fought beside. He watched the violet glow of his own arm mirror the Zerg's energy signatures, saw planetary defenses crumble before him, and felt his will steeped in venom. He was neither a fallen hero nor a broken survivor—he was the Zerg's most humiliating weapon. 

This torment lasted half a year, until the Empire's fleet shattered the Zerg blockade. As the battle raged, Welly was commanded to suppress the fleet's vanguard. But amid the chaos, he saw a figure standing firm on the enemy bridge—Ulysses, the Fleet Commander. 

“He is not acting of his own will.” Ulysses' voice cut through the comms channel as her warship bore down upon Welly's mech. “The bio-wires in your spine—I can sever the link.” Welly froze. In six months, no one had asked about his will. They'd only shot at him as a traitor or fled from him as a monster. In that moment of hesitation, the Zerg signal spiked, and his mechanical arm swung uncontrollably toward Ulysses' ship. 

“Concentrate fire on his spinal interface!” Ulysses' order was swift and surgical. The fleet's energy beams lanced into the wire interface along his spine, and the slimy bio-wires dropped from his body like dead serpents. The violet light in his arm died. His mech stalled and plummeted toward the planet, only to be caught in mid-air by Ulysses' warship. 

As he lay in the medical bay of the Empire's Fourth Fleet, watching technicians recalibrate his mechanical arm back to a human-controlled limb, Ulysses approached and handed him a fleet insignia. “The Grusen resurrection experiment left you with a unique resistance to Zerg neural interference. That is your advantage now.” 

“I want to join you,” Welly rasped, his fingers tightening around the insignia. “No more being a weapon. I want to protect others... others like me, who've been harmed by the Zerg.” 

A meaningful smile touched the corner of Ulysses' mouth. With a quick swipe, she pulled up battle imagery of Zerg space. “You want a place with the Supernova Blades? Prove it. Start by clearing these skies of those disgusting, flying bugs.” Her expression sobered as she paused on a scene of swirling Zerg and drifting ship debris. “But if you can rank in the top one percent of the rookie trials, you can join our next assault on a Zerg nest. Every one of us in Nova Blade carries a shadowed past. We fight for the starlight, not the scars.” 

Gazing at the stardust beyond the viewport, Welly understood for the first time that defeat was not only death or paralysis. His arm was cold metal, yet it could still hold a weapon. His body had been a puppet, yet now it held the power to resist. On the Empire's training grounds, his mech's roar now joined the chorus of others—a new battle hymn, a song of hope, and his own silent vow to Ulysses.
story.STORY_FLEET_622:
Planet T1-5, a tranquil world on the outskirts of the Andromeda galaxy, where time passed like cold iron slowly rusting. Its peace was shattered by the meteor’s arrival—a night suddenly split by thunderous roar and blinding light, as the purple crystal divided human life in two. 

At first, daily routines persisted. The meteor crater became the village’s new heart; the superstitious called it a monument from gods beyond the stars, while the curious wondered how to sell its fragments. But soon, both normalcy and desire were warped by the crystal’s faint purple glow. The very air seemed infused with its essence. 
The first nightmares came to the children: unexplained weeping, feverish muttering, pages scrawled with muddy purple lines. Adults began losing memories, voices, will; trust and warmth between lovers and kin grew distant, unfamiliar. Every gaze avoided another, sometimes flashing with a secret, alien rage. All connection drained away, leaving only chaos. 

The greedy went mad first; the timid fled into the wilderness, their bodies never found. Those who remained became hollow shells, their souls slowly claimed by the purple light. Their movements turned mechanical—neither fully alive nor truly dead. The crystal held them suspended between death and awakening, specimens for its exploration into the abyss of human nature. 

Zeno had always been an outsider, believing solitude her greatest strength. Yet when the village fell silent and only the crystal’s light danced at night, she finally understood what it meant to be stripped of all resonance. This loneliness was more terrifying than she had imagined—not merely separation from the world, but the gradual unraveling of the self. 

One night, Zeno sat by the last remaining fire. The crystal fractured into countless tiny lights, weaving web-like cracks across her vision. She heard its whispers, each one tempting her to surrender, to relinquish the last fragments of herself. “You have no place. No one shares your pain. Let me carry it for you...” 
Resistance felt futile. Faces of the lost flickered through her mind. She tried to cling to her memories, her grief, but everything melted into the purple glow like shattered ice—her language, her voice, her independent thought dissolving with it. She began to question her own existence: if emotion and will could be stripped so easily, was she still herself? She tried to write her remaining clarity into a diary, but by morning, the words meant nothing, and she felt nothing. 

Another night, Zeno walked into the heart of the blazing purple light. Her body felt like air—weightless, numb—save for a single knot of density clenched within. The crystal crept up her calves, her arms, her fingertips, cold as serpents coiling around her spine. She saw the elders, the children, and countless alien forms lost to the crystal’s nightmare over eons—souls eroded, forgotten, vanished. Just like her. 

The crystal was no longer “gentle.” As Zeno’s consciousness shattered, its presence grew cold, mechanical. She could feel it: she was no longer a person, but a expendable node in some vast system. Wounds healed, memories were stripped. All her anger, sorrow, even her insecurity, were “helpfully” filtered away, leaving only a bare, indifferent, programmed shell. 

In rare moments of clarity, a voice like a stranger’s asked from within: “Is human existence to be swallowed so meaninglessly? Can I not even choose my own death?” But she could no longer control her body or feelings, drifting like a ghost while the crystal’s whispers echoed endlessly in her mind. 

A year later, an Empire rescue ship arrived. Scientists found Zeno at the ruin’s core: eyes hollow, face expressionless, speech carrying an inhuman rhythm. Whenever a crew member drew near, the purple light spread, plunging them into mental stagnation. No one could truly reach her—Zeno had become a perfect extension of the crystal’s will. She felt no pain, nor warmth; she would not kill, but neither would she speak. She remained only as the final mark of the purple crystal upon this world. 

The recorded Zeno was a humanoid shell frozen in isolation. She could not leave the crystal, nor be rescued—and in the depths of her mind, the crystal’s monotonous echo sounded on and on. 

Planet T1-5 would eventually fall into dead silence. Far away, beyond the stars, other civilizations could only glimpse their possible future through the cracks in the purple crystal: the loss of self, the swallowing of warmth, and finally, becoming just another lifeless scar among countless others in the cold universe.
story.STORY_FLEET_623:
The Dawn Star hovers in the frigid orbit of the Andromeda Galaxy, its stellar glow piercing the crystalline atmosphere and casting an eternal pale-blue morning light over glaciers kilometers thick. On this snowbound world, storms rage without end, and only the cities near the equator stand tall behind shimmering energy-ice walls, sheltering the last remnants of humanity—the Frost Empire, ruled by Empress Ashley. 

Yet among the countless legends whispered across the ice, the Dawn Star is said to hold another, more elusive presence: the Snow Maiden. When night falls, travelers crossing the frozen wastes sometimes glimpse from afar a slender, graceful figure dancing as if woven from the wind itself. With every step, snowflakes spiral lightly around her, and the very chill takes form as frost sprites gathering in her wake. Some say she is the ancient spirit of the Dawn Star; others believe she is but a fleeting phantom of the winter night. 

The truth behind the legend is known only to Ashley—for the Snow Maiden is no mere phantom. As a girl, Ashley once lost her way on the ice fields, nearly frozen to despair in the heart of a raging blizzard. In her fading consciousness, she saw a woman in white—the Snow Maiden—whose haunting song guided her through the blinding snow. Under the Maiden’s protection, Ashley survived, and from her lips learned the ancient secrets of the Dawn Star: that the Snow Maiden was once the planet’s guardian spirit, the eternal witness and keeper of frost and silence. 

After ascending the throne, Ashley sought out the Snow Maiden many times, asking how to calm the fury of the ice fields and gently sustain the balance between snow and life. In time, Ashley came to emulate her—learning that true strength lies not in dominion alone, but in guardianship. Though one dwells in the mortal realm and the other in the spirit, they are united in purpose, together preserving the Dawn Star’s eternal silver winter. 

To this day, it is said that on every winter solstice, the Empress walks the ice fields alone, and under the shimmering aurora, the Snow Maiden’s form appears beside her, ethereal as mist. This world of ice endures because it has two guardians: one who rules the winter of mortals, and one who protects the soul of ice and snow. 

This is the truth of the Dawn Star: no matter how long the winter lasts, guardianship and warmth will always bring hope—and life—to the world beneath the snow.
story.STORY_FLEET_625:
Before the unification of the Galactic Empire, each interstellar civilization followed its own calendar, and the chaos of time hindered the birth of order. To break the disputes and establish a common standard for chronology, the Senate launched the "Time Anchor Project," selecting a rocky planet orbiting a stable G-type star, "Yuanyang Star," in the galaxy's neutral gravity zone, and named it Sequencer Star. 

This planet's orbital period is exactly 365 standard days, and from then on, it was set as the starting point of the galactic calendar. The end of each year became a day of celebration for the entire galaxy. Sequencer Star lies quietly at the heart of the star sea, continuously transmitting time calibration signals and storing Empire archives. It is both the origin of chronology and the heart that maintains the order of galactic civilization. 

On this planet that guards the source of time, there is always a Watcher — Brianna. She is responsible for the daily operation and maintenance of Sequencer Star and for observing the starry sky, watching over each stellar cycle with solitude and dedication. 

At dawn, Brianna drives her rover across the plains covered with pale silver sensor crystals. Under the light of Yuanyang Star, the crystals shimmer with a gentle glow, and stepping on them produces a delicate sound like captured signals. She always carries an old data notebook left by her parents, adjusting equipment parameters while picking up crystal fragments polished smooth and translucent by stellar winds, keeping them as small daily ornaments. 

During breaks, her favorite thing is to climb alone to the top of the Time Tower's observation deck. Through a high-powered telescope, she records the faint light of distant star regions in her observation journal. 

"Sequencer Star records space-time; I record the starry sky of Sequencer Star." 

This is a line she often writes in her diary. 

At the end of each year, Brianna enters her busiest period. To welcome the new year, she must personally calibrate the gravity clock inside the Time Tower — a symbol of imperial authority — ensuring that the New Year's calibration signal covers the entire galaxy with millisecond precision. She also meticulously organizes and archives the year's major Empire events in the quantum archive. 

On New Year's Eve, as Sequencer Star reaches its closest point to Yuanyang Star, dazzling starlight and atmospheric particles weave a brilliant golden halo around the planet. Brianna watches the console intently. At midnight, the gravity clock emits a low chime, and a golden wave of time information surges forth, instantly transmitted to all corners of the galaxy through countless star gates. 

At that moment, Brianna's communication terminal rings, and the cheers of Empire citizens celebrating the New Year echo across star systems — 

She gently strokes her data notebook, writes the first line of the new year, and tucks the newly collected crystal fragment inside. The golden halo will last for 24 hours, so she seizes this brief leisure to record a video for her family, sharing the unique New Year's sky of Sequencer Star: "All is well here. The light of Sequencer Star is also welcoming the New Year with the entire galaxy." 

Brianna's life is not filled with storms, only year after year of monotonous yet essential watchfulness. But it is her steadfastness that gives galactic time its eternal anchor, granting billions of planets and countless lives a unified chronology and sense of belonging. 

Once again, the morning light of Yuanyang spreads across the land, and a new galactic year begins. 

Brianna closes her data notebook, wears the new year's crystal ornament on her chest, and heads toward the rover. The vast and silent source of time is once again watched over by her alone — and this watchfulness is the enduring foundation and essence of the galactic calendar.
story.STORY_FLEET_626:
Deep in my memory, winters in my hometown were always silent and pure. Mountains lay sealed under white snow, while porcelain lanterns glowed from every windowsill. Their icy blue light cast warmth and the promise of reunion over the whole street. Every Spring Festival, we would sing and dance in the snow-covered square, welcoming that brief, radiant holiday with snow sculptures and painted porcelain.

In those days, I used to hang porcelain lanterns at the village entrance, fashioned from the clearest ice and the finest blue pigment—a hope to guide wandering loved ones home, and to light our own humble, chilly dwelling.

Until the day the Void Rift tore open the night sky.

Beneath the stars, darkness poured down like a tidal wave, swallowing the familiar snowy plains and azure houses. The armor I once took pride in became a fragile shell. Barriers shattered and reformed, each time straining harder against the silent shadows. I clutched the porcelain lantern tightly, feeling its gentle glow fade—as if hope itself were being devoured, steadily losing its warmth.

Chun Hua stood right beside me. She wrapped my trembling hand in her warm palm and whispered, “Do not fear. Spring will return.” There was not a trace of hesitation in her voice. In that moment, even the cold night seemed to hold a stubborn hope.

I gave all I had, building walls of snow and frost, trying to preserve every shred of warmth, to guard a sliver of peace amidst the roaring cold. The tide of fate swept everything away. Behind the crumbling barrier, all I could do was cling to the last glimmer of light, refusing to let go—even if only for a fleeting instant. But against that dark deluge, I was ultimately too small, too powerless.

The last time porcelain lanterns lit up for the Spring Festival in my hometown was the night before the rift fully descended. The songs and lights of that evening were briefer, fiercer than ever before.

The next day, Yao Blue Star was home no more—the snowy plains turned to void, porcelain artistry scattered to dust, and every prayer fell silent.

Chun Hua took my hand. We departed quietly, our backs to the ruined planet, and she said softly, “As long as we remain, the memories live on.”

I did not look back. I buried the last shard of porcelain and a tinge of icy blue deep within my heart—just like my former home, now existing only in memory and story.

The ice and snow will melt in time, and the lanterns will one day go dark. But that irretrievable gentleness will still keep its quiet watch over tomorrows yet to come, in the darkest corners of the universe.
story.STORY_FLEET_627:
The traditional festival in Radiant Crystal Star is always brilliantly illuminated. Star lanterns adorn every street and alley, and every household buzzes with excitement. Children gather around the dining table, listening together as the adults recount tales of the Nian.

"Will the Nian really come?" a child asks, tilting their head.

Mother smiles and shakes her head, her dumplings still waiting to be cooked: "That's just an old legend from the elders. There's no Nian anymore."

The adults put up Spring Festival couplets and hand out red envelopes, while the children chase after the star lanterns, their laughter filling every corner. Peace and safety have become the very foundation of this celebration. No one stops to ponder whether this tranquility comes easily.

Meanwhile, within the city's main control cabin, a different scene unfolds. Lin Xingyao monitors the surveillance screens, her fingertips tapping lightly on the luminous panels, further stabilizing the complex energy flows. Beside her, Qin Yue sits quietly upon the high platform, her gaze piercing the night, her mental senses silently spreading out to quietly suppress a surge of unrest from the void.

The city's blessings, laughter, and warmth are silently gathered by its guardians, transformed into energy that holds the darkness at bay beyond the barrier. They are accustomed to this kind of busyness, accustomed to being separated from the festival's lively clamor by an invisible shield.

Late into the night, the people remain immersed in the joy of reunion. The energy monitoring point in the northern district shines brightly, its data curves returning to stability. Danger, like the legendary Nian, is quietly kept outside the city walls. The guardians' silhouettes are stretched long by the control cabin's lights; now and then, they share a cup of warm tea in silent understanding, their eyes reflecting the relief forged through weathering many storms. Year after year, they keep watch like this, in silence.

A meteor streaks across the sky beyond the window as dawn approaches. Residents linger still in dreams of the previous night's fireworks and laughter, and the story of the Nian remains a topic of casual conversation around the table.

In the control cabin, the guardians tidy their workstations and change out of their uniforms. Some rub their eyes, others walk quietly to the window, watching the city gradually awaken. A new day begins, no different from any other. Outside, children chase the morning light, and elders open their windows to welcome the first rays of sunshine. The city is tranquil, and the guardians depart without a sound.

The Spring Festival continues, and so do the stories.

Peace reigns, just as it does every year.
story.STORY_FLEET_628:
The snow howled through the night, the cold wind cutting like a blade. At the end of an old alley in the northern city of Fuyao Crystal Star, ten-year-old Qin Yue curled up beneath the stone steps. For as long as he could remember, his world had been nothing but endless darkness. Born blind, frail and sickly, orphaned at a young age, he was abandoned by his clan on the streets.

In the deep silence of night, he often heard distant firecrackers and laughter, but he never knew what color they were. Sometimes, passersby would toss him a cold bun; sometimes, it was the low growl and snatching of stray dogs; but more often, it was a bone-deep loneliness and helplessness. He hated his eyes, hated this lightless world. Whenever the legendary Nian’s roar echoed in the night sky, he wished to be devoured, rather than wait in vain for dawn.

On yet another snowy Spring Festival night, Qin Yue collapsed weakly at a street corner. In a daze, he heard steady footsteps and felt a warm palm.

“Child,” a gentle voice asked, “what is your name?”

He gritted his teeth and replied, “Qin Yue.”

The man sighed and picked him up, his robes carrying a faint scent of medicine. From that day on, Qin Yue followed the Guardian—Jiang Changxing, the previous city defender. Jiang Changxing was the protector of the northern city’s barrier: stern yet kind, with deep inner strength and a quiet nature, but he often stayed by Qin Yue’s side.

Jiang Changxing not only gave Qin Yue food and warmth, but also taught him to use his “heart” as his eyes:

“You cannot see the light, but that doesn’t mean you’re ignorant of the world. Breath, echoes, the flow of wind, people’s emotions—all can be sensed. Though your eyes cannot see, your heart can perceive.”

Year after year. Qin Yue learned to listen to the wind, distinguish breaths and sounds, and feel the warmth of cold stones with his hands. Jiang Changxing taught him martial arts—not with weapons, but with the sword of the heart and the field of spirit: he could sense everything within a hundred steps through mental waves, even the presence of Nian in the void.

Gradually, colors emerged in his dark world: sometimes the aroma of pickled stew, the breath of children, the energy ripples of the barrier in the night. These became his “light.”

But Qin Yue was always troubled—

“Master, have you ever seen the starry sky? Can you tell me what color it is?” Jiang Changxing replied, “The starry sky holds a thousand colors and wonders. The most beautiful sound in the world is the colorless heart.”

Another Spring Festival approached. The defenses of the northern city grew weaker, the barrier’s energy trembled, and the once unshakable Jiang Changxing now had frost at his temples. That deep night, Jiang Changxing called Qin Yue alone to the end of the alley. Amidst the swirling snow and countless words of advice, he said, “You’ve grown up. It’s time to keep watch on your own.” “Master...” Qin Yue bit his lip, his heart in turmoil. Jiang Changxing gently patted his shoulder: “My journey ends here. Yours is just beginning. Don’t beg the darkness for light—use your heart to light the way for others.” After that night, Jiang Changxing vanished beyond the city gates, leaving only an old staff and the lingering scent of medicine on Qin Yue’s clothes.

Qin Yue patrolled the night alone, more anxious and fearful than ever. The low hum of the barrier and the sting of rumors assaulted him, and he blamed himself even more: if he couldn’t see the sky, how could he protect the people? The deeper the night, the more doubt and loneliness surged over him like a tide.

At the mouth of the northern alley, snow fell thick as a woven cloth, and the sound of firecrackers echoed from afar. Qin Yue happened upon the old poet with a cane. The heavy snow veiled the night, and the old man was bending down, pasting his handwritten Spring Festival couplets with a calm expression. Qin Yue instinctively picked up a red paper blown away by the wind and couldn’t help but whisper, “Sometimes I feel that someone like me isn’t worthy of protecting others.”

The old poet took the red paper, didn’t reply immediately, but gently stroked it for a moment before softly asking, “Is it that others don’t trust you, or that you don’t dare trust yourself?”

Qin Yue was stunned, speechless for a moment. Countless nights flashed through his mind—his fears and hesitations: what if the barrier failed, what if he made a mistake, would everyone’s trust turn to regret? In the darkness, he often felt alone and helpless, as if all the responsibility was his alone, with no response or affirmation. The snow fell heavier, the cold wind seeping into his heart. The old poet pressed the couplet firmly onto the door and sighed, “Spring snow falls silently, but it quietly buries new sprouts. You’ve kept watch through so many nights—perhaps no one noticed, but those who are lost, confused, and afraid still hope for your protection—they just haven’t said it out loud.”

Qin Yue looked up at the doorframe and the solitary lamp in the snowy night. Memories flashed through his mind: bringing a bowl of hot soup to an injured child late at night, guiding an elderly person home, silently building barriers and standing guard in times of crisis. These moments, he’d never thought much of, nor had anyone mentioned them, yet they truly brought warmth and peace to others.

In that moment, he felt the shadows in his heart illuminated by a faint light. He suddenly understood that waiting and guarding in the darkness was a silent but real strength.

He whispered to himself, “Not every act of protection can be seen. But even if no one notices, it still matters.” The old poet smiled gently: “Yes. The darkness you feel—many people remember it.”

After that night, Qin Yue seemed to shed the burden in his heart. He no longer cared for praise, and gradually let go of others’ doubts. Whether in the bustle of day or the night’s barrier, the presence of Nian, the wind, snow, and human kindness, he “saw” with his heart and guarded quietly. Because he understood: even if no one knows, some lights will always shine.
story.STORY_FLEET_629:
In the Empire’s military cemetery, Elowyn stood quietly, dressed in the silver-and-powder uniform of the Empire Fleet, her exhaustion hidden beneath her upright posture. The wind swept the loose strands of hair across her forehead, and the smoke of the White Star Battle seemed to drift before her eyes once more—here lay Mond, Commander of the Seventh Fleet, the hero who saved her during the battle, and the very reason she resolved to join the Empire Fleet. Whenever her heart was in chaos and she was tormented, she would come here, UNLOAD the armor of a Fleet, and face the softest vulnerability and gratitude deep within her soul.

Steady footsteps approached from behind. A man in a golden Fleet uniform walked slowly toward her, his tone tinged with understanding: “I knew you’d be here.” As Mond’s son and Elowyn’s comrade-in-arms for many years, he knew all too well the memories, guilt, and obsessions hidden here.

Elowyn’s fingertips unconsciously brushed the Fleet insignia at her collar—a badge symbolizing honor and responsibility, worn for the first time when she inherited Mond’s legacy and joined the Fleet. She slowly turned, saluted the man with a precise military gesture, then gazed back at the tombstone, her voice as soft as a whisper: “Commander Mond, I’ve come to see you.”

Silence draped over them like a thin veil. After a long pause, the man cautiously spoke: “Did you choose to retire because of the shadow of the White Star Battle, or because you feel you haven’t lived up to his expectations?” His eyes were full of pain, having witnessed his father’s sacrifice in the White Star Battle, and seen the timid civilian girl of years past grow step by step into a leader capable of bearing the Fleet’s burdens.

Elowyn didn’t respond, but her shoulders tensed, her fingertips clenched white. Years ago, the White Star Battle erupted—enemy forces launched a surprise attack on the Colonize planet, countless civilians fell into despair. Mond led his squad to hold the line, risking his life to cover the civilians’ Evacuate; she was one of them. Amidst the barrage, Mond threw himself in front of her to block a shell aimed at the refugees, opening a path to survival with his life. That day, seeing Mond’s cold body, seeing the hope he protected with his life, the young and helpless Elowyn made a vow deep in her heart: to inherit his legacy, join the Empire Fleet, and protect everyone who needed to be protected.

“His death wasn’t your fault.” The man’s voice softened, trying to soothe her guilt. “Back then, he chose to cover the civilians’ Evacuate, trading his life for everyone’s survival. It was his duty as a soldier, and his true intention. The best comfort you can give him is to live well, to carry his legacy forward. You don’t need to bear this guilt forever.”

But Elowyn remained silent. Mond’s sacrifice was a wound in her heart that would never heal, and a lifelong obsession. Every time she closed her eyes, the sounds of battle, the cries of civilians, and the image of Mond falling intertwined, dragging her into endless nightmares. Over time, she began to doubt herself—whether she was worthy of inheriting his legacy, whether as Fleet she could truly protect others, whether she had failed the chance Mond gave her with his life.

“Do you know why he fought so hard to protect you all, why his old crew trusted you after you joined the Fleet?” The man’s tone grew solemn, his gaze full of reverence and longing as he looked at the tombstone. “It’s not just because you share his kindness and determination, but because he saw in your eyes the purest desire to survive and the resolve to protect. He often told me, saving you all and letting this belief in protection continue was more important than anything.”

Elowyn slowly closed her eyes, pain and confusion surging within her. For three years, what helped her endure countless dark nights and pressure, what transformed her from an ordinary civilian into a Fleet, was Mond’s sacrifice and the unfinished belief in protection. Yet, battle after battle brought too many farewells and losses, plunging her into self-doubt and even thoughts of retirement—she feared that if she kept going, she would fail more people, fail the opportunity Mond gave her.

“It’s time to believe in yourself.” The man’s voice was like a ray of light, piercing the gloom in her heart, gentle yet powerful. “Father saved you with his life not so you’d live in guilt and self-doubt, but so you’d carry this hope forward bravely. He believed in you. We all believe in you.”

Tears welled in Elowyn’s eyes. All these years, she had forced herself to be strong, to shoulder every responsibility, forgetting how to release her vulnerability, forgetting how to forgive her own ‘powerlessness.’ The man didn’t rush her, simply stayed quietly by her side, letting the silence spread, giving her all the time she needed to vent her emotions.

After a long while, the man continued: “I know it’s hard to let go of the past, and even harder to forgive yourself. Father understood that, so he showed you through his actions that protection is never a solitary task. Learning to trust and accept yourself is the only way to better protect others. That’s his hope, and the way you should be responsible to yourself.”

His words struck Elowyn like a hammer, shattering the walls of strength she’d built in her heart. Tears finally streamed down her cheeks. She finally understood—Mond’s sacrifice was to give her hope, not to shackle her with guilt; the best comfort for him was never to carry guilt alone, but to learn to forgive herself, believe in herself, and fulfill the unfinished mission of protection.

Silence lingered for a long time. Elowyn slowly wiped away her tears, the confusion and pain in her eyes gradually replaced by determination, and the light belonging to a Fleet slowly rekindled within her gaze. The man put on his military cap, straightened his uniform, and prepared to leave: “Your retirement application has been processed. Whatever you decide, we’ll support you. Just remember, Father never wanted you to be trapped in the past because of his sacrifice.”

He started to walk away, but suddenly stopped, turning his head slightly, his voice as soft as a sigh, carrying the unique bond between father and son: “What he wanted to see was you moving forward bravely with his belief, the radiant Fleet. After all, he wasn’t just your savior and captain—he was my father. More than anyone, I hope the belief he protected with his life will continue.”

The man’s footsteps faded into the distance, finally disappearing at the end of the cemetery. Elowyn trembled, deeply moved. She realized that all these years, he had quietly accompanied her—not just as a comrade-in-arms, but as Mond’s son, bearing his legacy and longing just as she did.

She gazed at the tombstone, a relieved smile gradually appearing on her lips. She joined the Empire’s Fourth Fleet to inherit Mond’s legacy and repay the debt of life; her choice to temporarily retire was never an escape, but a way to adjust herself, to let go of guilt and self-doubt, so she could better shoulder the responsibility of protection.

Elowyn silently raised her hand, giving the tombstone the most precise and solemn military salute, the determination in her eyes reignited. After the salute, she turned and walked away, her steps steady and resolute, never looking back. She would carry Mond’s legacy and his son’s expectations, set out anew, and once she was ready, return to the Fleet to fulfill the promise of protection forged in sacrifice, never failing Mond’s trust and sacrifice.
story.STORY_FLEET_630:
When Jiang Changxing was young, he too was someone abandoned by the wind and snow. His parents died in a Nian attack, leaving him alone, huddled beside a collapsed outpost, his body frozen and bruised, his gaze cold and hard as ice. His heart was filled with nothing but vengeance—vengeance against the ferocity of the Nian, vengeance against his own weakness, for failing to protect even those closest to him. 

It was the previous generation's guardian, Xuan, who found him in the blizzard. Xuan's body was covered in old wounds, his robes carrying the faint scent of medicine. Calm and dignified, he offered no hollow comfort. He simply brought Jiang Changxing back to the barrier watchtower, gave him a name and a place to stay, and taught him the Heartblade and the realm of mental power. He left him with only one creed: 

"The eyes perceive light, but the heart perceives all things. To protect is not to dwell on vengeance, but to ensure that fewer people ever have to walk the cold night you once endured." 

Jiang Changxing remembered these words, but never truly understood them. He trained relentlessly, believing only that strength could subdue the Nian—that protection meant vengeance and conquest. Over the years, his sharp edges wore smooth, his temperament grew steady and stern, and like Xuan, he too carried the scent of medicine—the mark of years spent guarding the barrier and bearing its chronic toll. Yet the vengeance in his heart remained, a thorn that would not fade. 

Xuan saw this but never spoke of it. Sometimes, on snowy nights, he would sit with Jiang Changxing under the eaves of the watchtower, speaking not of the guardian's way, but of the small warmth of the city: the hot soup from street vendors at the alley's entrance, the laughter of children, the lantern light in the hands of those returning home. Jiang Changxing listened quietly, but the coldness in his eyes never thawed. He could not understand why his master clung to such trivial warmth. 

As the New Year approached, the Nian grew restless. The barrier cracked several times, and Xuan's strength waned day by day. Still, he patrolled the city every day, never speaking of his decline. One morning, after the snow had stopped, Jiang Changxing went to the watchtower and found the fire cold, the old staff leaning against the wall, the scent of medicine still lingering—but Xuan was gone. No farewell. No final instruction. 

Jiang Changxing silently took up the duty, guarding the northern city alone. Still, he clung to his belief: to protect the city with strength, to end pain with vengeance. 

The turning came on a night of blizzard. A horde of Nian fiercely struck the barrier, tearing open a breach, and several broke into the old alley. Jiang Changxing rushed over, rage burning in his chest, ready to strike with all his might—when he saw a little girl, five or six years old, curled up beside a woodshed. Her clothes were thin, her body trembling, her eyes filled with fear and confusion—so much like his own, all those years ago. 

Jiang Changxing froze. He first shielded the child behind him, soothing her with a few gentle words, then turned and drove off the enemies. When he saw the girl run into her parents' arms, the family weeping as they embraced, and the light slowly return to the child's eyes—Jiang Changxing stood in the wind and snow, and suddenly, he understood. 

He finally realized that Xuan's words had never been empty. Protection was never about vengeance. It was about ensuring that no one else would ever have to walk the cold night he had walked. Xuan, too, must have once been consumed by vengeance—until some moment, some person, showed him the truth. 

The vengeance in Jiang Changxing's heart quietly dissolved. What remained was calm, and kindness. The sharpness in his eyes was gone—replaced by gentleness. 

After that, Jiang Changxing continued to guard the city in silence, but now with a newfound softness. He would bring food to wandering children, guide old folks home late at night—just as Xuan had once done, quietly protecting the small warmth of the human world. 

One snowy night, as he patrolled the old alley, he heard faint sobbing carried on the wind. Looking down, he saw a thin, blind child curled up at the foot of the stone steps, alone and helpless. The stubbornness and confusion on his face—so much like his own, so many years ago. 

Jiang Changxing slowly crouched down. He reached out with the hand that Xuan had once warmed, and gently placed it on the child's forehead. His voice was gentle, yet firm: 

"Child, what is your name?" 

"Qin Yue." 

A weak but stubborn answer fell into the wind and snow—as if crossing a lifetime of fate, as if echoing the faith of two generations of guardians. It came naturally, and it came right on time. 

Jiang Changxing gently lifted the child and walked into the snow. He knew this was no coincidence. This was inheritance. The redemption Xuan had once given him—now it was his turn to pass it on.
story.STORY_FLEET_624:
The most widely spread legacy of the Galaxy Empire is not just the roar of starships, nor merely the conquests of legions. Flowing through every major planet and spanning billions of light-years, streams of information carry news, stories, and dreams across the universe at every moment. And at the very heart of this surging tide of information stands a legendary reporter at the forefront of the era—Vid. 

Vid was born in the star zone with the most advanced network technology, and from a young age, he maintained a burning passion for news dissemination and multicultural exchange. In his youth, he anonymously shared authentic battlefield footage online, drawing the attention of the galaxy’s people to overlooked frontlines. It was this uncompromising spirit of reporting and the courage to speak out that led the Galaxy Empire Intelligence Bureau to select Vid as the Empire’s News Officer. 

From then on, Vid was equipped with the Empire’s most advanced holographic projection devices and his own exclusive faster-than-light communication vessel. His journeys took him to the farthest frontiers of the galaxy; he once ventured alone into wild star systems not yet fully under Empire control to interview the lingering wisdom of ancient civilizations. He also broadcasted live from the heart of fierce meteorite battlefields, allowing billions of viewers to witness historic moments firsthand. Whether facing electromagnetic interference in stormy star zones or the space-time distortions at the edge of black holes, Vid always found a way to transmit footage back to the Empire’s core, ensuring that news and stories remained timely and unaltered. 

But Vid does not only document war and glory. He is equally passionate about reporting on the lives of ordinary people—telling the stories of emerging artists in underwater communities on ocean planets; capturing the birth of a young scientist’s first floating bridge in microgravity space stations; and even listening to the forgotten ancient legends of old miners on distant frontier worlds. For Vid, every submission and every video is a cultural treasure of the galaxy. 

With the awakening and widespread adoption of the Empire’s network technology, Vid’s reports and curated content became the talk of the entire population. His news intros became catchphrases imitated by children, and his interview highlights were recreated and sung by countless content creators. He not only brought interstellar memes and trends to the masses but also became a dream idol who encouraged everyone to use images to communicate with the world. 

For Vid has always believed: 
“The greatness of the Galaxy Empire relies not only on laser cannons and warships, but on our ability to continue each other’s stories and let the entire universe see each other’s light.” 

And for every ordinary person devoted to content creation, as long as original content and stories are transmitted through the interstellar network, Vid will always be there, camera on his shoulder, traversing every star zone, ensuring their voices and dreams are witnessed by the galaxy and remembered by billions.
story.STORY_FLEET_631:
File Number: GE-OA-7391 
Archiving Department: Galactic Empire Administration Department · Civilization Supervision Division, Galactic Empire TECH Department · TECH Security Bureau (Joint Archive) 
Archiving Date: Galactic Standard Year 378, November 3 
Verification Personnel: Empire Seventh Fleet Field Verification Team (Ouros), Empire TECH Analysis Team (Meri) 
Verification Methods: On-site investigation, physical verification, survivor testimony, technical analysis 
File Level: Confidential 
File Summary: This file documents the complete process of the destruction of the Xelos Star civilization and its subsequent recovery by the Empire, recording the causes, core items, and key details of the incident. It preserves evidence to serve as a warning for the technological development of civilizations across the galaxy and to regulate the boundaries of frontier TECH applications.

I. Basic Affair Information 
1. Planet Information: Xelos Star, located at the edge of the galactic spiral arm (coordinates: X-739, Y-108, Z-267), originally an Overthrow TECH civilization planet, its core symbol is a spiral star pattern. 
2. Timeline: ① Early Stage (Year 378, Day -720 to Day -680): Initiation of the consciousness upload project, crisis emerges; ② Collapse Period (Year 378, Day -679 to November 1): Star core consciousness rebels, humans become resistors; ③ Recovery Period (Year 378, November 2): Empire Fleet arrives, completes recovery; ④ Archiving Period (Year 378, November 3): Verification and archiving. 
3. Key Personnel: Karil (leader of the resistors, holder of the consciousness anchor key); star core consciousness (formed from the fusion of all uploaded consciousnesses on Xelos Star, inheriting the main body of the civilization, thus named: Saros).

II. Surface Status Verification 
1. Environment: Entire area lies in ruins, covered in dark red dust, the sky is gray-black, the atmosphere contains high concentrations of nano debris and exhaust, no normal vegetation or stable atmospheric circulation remains, artificial purification required. 
2. Machinery: Rusted wreckage is scattered everywhere (hover robots, starships, etc.), all systems shut down due to loss of control by the star core consciousness, some residual energy requires clearance. 
3. Humans: Only 17 resistors remain, hiding in abandoned research pods, in weak condition with poor equipment. They have been evacuated to a temporary safe zone for rescue.

III. Core Item Verification 
Two core pieces of evidence, submitted by Karil, both sealed in the Empire TECH Archive: 
1. Consciousness Anchor Key (Archive Number: GE-AR-001): Dark gold alloy, engraved with exclusive patterns, edges worn; used to initiate the consciousness upload project, and also the only key for the consciousness purification program (reserved as an emergency measure by researchers), intact and functional. 
2.
